extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in cultural criticism, social philosophy, and Victorian-era essays
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing English social classes (aristocracy, middle-class/Philistines, working-class/Populace) with respect to culture, authority, and the pursuit of 'sweetness and light' (the best self). The text offers evaluative distinctions (mean, excess, defect) and prescriptions for cultivating authority and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as pursuit of perfection ('sweetness and light')
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is the study of perfection: the love and pursuit of perfection, nurtured by reading, observing, and thinking; culture seeks to develop the 'best self' and produces 'sweetness and light'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture is not mere exterior accomplishments but the development of inward powers; it is the true nurse of the pursuing love of perfection and the source of the 'best self' which can furnish legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best self / right reason as legitimate authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper centre of authority should be the 'best self' or right reason — impersonal, united, and trustworthy — rather than the ordinary self or class-instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should 'never go against the best light you have; secondly, take care that your light be not darkness.' The State can legitimately act as organ of the collective best self when conscience testifies that it serves right reason rather than class advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ordinary self from best self
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary self affirms immediate impulses and class-based preferences ('doing as one likes'); it is inadequate as a basis for authority or for establishing strict standards of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the ordinary self as paramount; recognize when an impulse is merely class-instinct or 'machinery' (business, tea-meetings, deputations) rather than a pursuit of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the mean/excess/defect analytic method
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate social qualities, examine the virtuous mean, the excess, and the defect for each class or quality (e.g., aristocratic chivalry as mean, Sir Thomas Bateson's resistance as excess, a timid inaptitude as defect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this threefold test when judging representative figures: identify the mean (virtuous model), the excess (overreach), and the defect (failure or lack) to gain clearness in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic class: exterior culture and insufficiency of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy's culture is chiefly exterior — politeness, splendour, prowess, good looks — and tends to be inaccessible to deeper ideas; its insufficiency lies in a lack of inner 'light' or soul beneath outward gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the value of their external graces but critique the lack of deeper intellectual or moral cultivation; ideal politeness should have more 'soul' for perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-class (Philistine) character: self-reliance, machinery, and illiberal tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-class's strength is self-reliance and the machinery of business, chapels, tea-meetings, and addresses; they often prefer these external structures to 'sweetness and light' and may resist higher culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique the Philistine tendency to substitute practical machinery and comfort for inward perfection; note both their capacity for great works and the danger of philistine narrowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working-class qualities: inchoate honesty, ready action, need of culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The working-class shows honesty and ready powers of sympathy and action but often lacks sufficient 'light' gained by reading, observing, and thinking; these powers are 'inchoate and untrained'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cultivation (education, reading, reflection) to transform ready energies into enlightened action; beware of untrained excesses (iconoclasm, intemperate talk) that can lead to danger and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification taxonomy: Barbarians, Philistines, Populace
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical nomenclature for the three classes: Barbarians (aristocratic, exterior culture, love of liberty and sports), Philistines (middle-class, industrial machinery, business-orientation), Populace (raw, half-developed masses prone to disorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these labels to clarify social analysis while remembering individuals often contain mixed elements; the taxonomy is a heuristic, not an absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of 'aliens' within classes who pursue perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Within every class there exist persons led by the love of perfection ('genius' or humane spirit) who transcend their class-instincts and pursue the best self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and encourage these individuals; their presence moderates class-life and helps elicit culture that can spread beyond class boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an authoritative centre in literature and religion (a scale of value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society lacks clear authoritative centres (e.g., an Academy) to set high standards; readers often lack sense of a scale of value for judgments in literature or religion and treat locally popular organs as equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate recognition of higher and lower authorities of taste and thought; teach readers to distinguish more authoritative judgments (closer to an ideal centre) from inferior ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate taste for the sublime over the bathos
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural 'taste of the bathos' implanted in human nature; culture's role is to reorient taste so men 'relish the sublime' rather than remain satisfied with triviality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist customs and examples that encourage relish for the trivial; foster examples, instruction, and institutions that elevate taste toward the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as organ of collective best self, not class power
rubrics_metrics.description: When conceived rightly, the State should embody the collective best self and can therefore be trusted with authority; the fear of State power stems from imagining it as merely the class in control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accept State authority, ensure it is perceived as serving right reason impartially, not as a tool for one class's self-affirmation; support provisional strengthening of the executive when conscience shows it secures the common best interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as test for legitimacy of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience can testify whether the light one follows is truly the best light (right reason) or merely 'darkness' (class interest or error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before endorsing authority (individuals or institutions), apply the conscience-test: is their power exercised on behalf of impartial, humane ends or merely to affirm class advantages?

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to needless tumult and demonstrations when they threaten order
rubrics_metrics.description: The best self 'plainly enjoins us to set our faces against' multitudinous processions and unnecessary demonstrations that risk tumult and disorder during times of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support measures that prevent disorder when such measures are grounded in the pursuit of the common good and right reason, while guarding against measures that serve only class repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware equating numbers and force with truth or authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Large followings or armed strength (e.g., '200,000 souls' or '20,000 rifles') do not, by themselves, confer seriousness or moral authority on doctrines or leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply stricter moral and intellectual tests to doctrines rather than relying on popularity or strength; presence of many adherents or force is not a substitute for truth or enlightened authority.
